prompt: For real functions $f,g$ defined on the positive integers, their *Dirichlet convolution* is $(f*g)(n)=\sum_{k\mid n}f(k)\,g(n/k)$, the sum over all positive divisors $k$ of $n$. The function $\epsilon$ is $\epsilon(1)=1$ and $\epsilon(n)=0$ for $n\ne1$; $\mathbf 1(n)=1$ for all $n$; $U$ is the set of real functions $f$ with $f(1)\ne0$; and $f^{-1}$ is an inverse of $f$ if $f*f^{-1}=\epsilon$. Let $A(n)=1$ if $n=2^k$ for some integer $k\ge0$ and $A(n)=0$ otherwise, and let $B(n)=n$. Find a simple formula for $(A*B)(n)$ in terms of the prime factorization $n=2^{k_1}3^{k_2}5^{k_3}\cdots$.

solutions.title: Sum over powers of 2
solutions.body:
The only divisors $k$ of $n$ with $A(k)\ne0$ are $k=2^j$ for $0\le j\le k_1$, so $$(A*B)(n)=\sum_{j=0}^{k_1}\frac n{2^j}=n\left(1+\tfrac12+\cdots+\tfrac1{2^{k_1}}\right)=2^{k_1}\left(2-2^{-k_1}\right)\cdot3^{k_2}5^{k_3}\cdots=(2^{k_1+1}-1)\,3^{k_2}5^{k_3}\cdots.$$ Check: $n=2$ gives $A(1)B(2)+A(2)B(1)=3=2^2-1$.

**Answer: $(2^{k_1+1}-1)3^{k_2}5^{k_3}\cdots$**

reviewNote: Official solution states (2^{k1}-1)3^{k2}5^{k3}...; the correct factor is 2^{k1+1}-1 (e.g. n=2 gives 3, not 1).

prompt: For real functions $f,g$ defined on the positive integers, their *Dirichlet convolution* is $(f*g)(n)=\sum_{k\mid n}f(k)\,g(n/k)$, the sum over all positive divisors $k$ of $n$. The function $\epsilon$ is $\epsilon(1)=1$ and $\epsilon(n)=0$ for $n\ne1$; $\mathbf 1(n)=1$ for all $n$; $U$ is the set of real functions $f$ with $f(1)\ne0$; and $f^{-1}$ is an inverse of $f$ if $f*f^{-1}=\epsilon$. Prove that Dirichlet convolution is commutative ($f*g=g*f$) and associative ($f*(g*h)=(f*g)*h$).
answer: Commutativity: substitute $d=n/k$. Associativity: both sides equal $\sum_{abc=n}f(a)g(b)h(c)$.

solutions.title: Rewrite as sums over factorizations
solutions.body:
Commutativity: as $k$ runs over the divisors of $n$, so does $d=n/k$, hence $\sum_{k\mid n}f(k)g(n/k)=\sum_{d\mid n}f(n/d)g(d)=(g*f)(n)$.

Associativity: $$(f*(g*h))(n)=\sum_{a\mid n}f(a)\sum_{b\mid n/a}g(b)h\!\left(\tfrac n{ab}\right)=\sum_{(a,b,c):\,abc=n}f(a)g(b)h(c),$$ because choosing $a\mid n$ and then $b\mid n/a$ is the same as choosing an ordered triple of positive integers with product $n$ (with $c=n/(ab)$). By the same argument $((f*g)*h)(n)=\sum_{c\mid n}h(c)\sum_{a\mid n/c}f(a)g\!\left(\tfrac n{ac}\right)$ equals the same triple sum. So the two are equal. ∎

prompt: For real functions $f,g$ defined on the positive integers, their *Dirichlet convolution* is $(f*g)(n)=\sum_{k\mid n}f(k)\,g(n/k)$, the sum over all positive divisors $k$ of $n$. The function $\epsilon$ is $\epsilon(1)=1$ and $\epsilon(n)=0$ for $n\ne1$; $\mathbf 1(n)=1$ for all $n$; $U$ is the set of real functions $f$ with $f(1)\ne0$; and $f^{-1}$ is an inverse of $f$ if $f*f^{-1}=\epsilon$. Show that $\epsilon$ is an identity for Dirichlet convolution, i.e. $(\epsilon*f)(n)=f(n)$ for every $f$ and $n$, and that no other function has this property.
answer: $(\epsilon*f)(n)=f(n)$ because only the term $k=1$ survives; if $e$ is also an identity then $e=e*\epsilon=\epsilon$.

solutions.title: Direct computation and uniqueness
solutions.body:
$(\epsilon*f)(n)=\sum_{k\mid n}\epsilon(k)f(n/k)$; only $k=1$ gives a nonzero $\epsilon(k)$, so the sum is $f(n)$. By commutativity also $f*\epsilon=f$.

If $e$ is another function with $e*f=f$ for all $f$, then taking $f=\epsilon$ gives $e*\epsilon=\epsilon$. But $e*\epsilon=e$ (since $\epsilon$ is an identity and convolution is commutative), so $e=\epsilon$. ∎

prompt: For real functions $f,g$ defined on the positive integers, their *Dirichlet convolution* is $(f*g)(n)=\sum_{k\mid n}f(k)\,g(n/k)$, the sum over all positive divisors $k$ of $n$. The function $\epsilon$ is $\epsilon(1)=1$ and $\epsilon(n)=0$ for $n\ne1$; $\mathbf 1(n)=1$ for all $n$; $U$ is the set of real functions $f$ with $f(1)\ne0$; and $f^{-1}$ is an inverse of $f$ if $f*f^{-1}=\epsilon$. Show that every $f\in U$ has an inverse by describing a process for computing it (a full inductive definition is not required), and prove that the inverse is unique.
answer: Existence: solve $(f*f^{-1})(n)=\epsilon(n)$ for $f^{-1}(n)$ successively: $f^{-1}(1)=1/f(1)$ and $f^{-1}(n)=-\frac1{f(1)}\sum_{k\mid n,k>1}f(k)f^{-1}(n/k)$. Uniqueness: $g_1=g_1*(f*g_2)=(g_1*f)*g_2=g_2$.

solutions.title: Existence by recursion
solutions.body: The equation $(f*f^{-1})(1)=1$ reads $f(1)f^{-1}(1)=1$, so $f^{-1}(1)=1/f(1)$ (this is why $f(1)\ne0$ is needed). For $n>1$, $(f*f^{-1})(n)=0$ reads $$f(1)f^{-1}(n)+\sum_{k\mid n,\,k>1}f(k)f^{-1}(n/k)=0,$$ and every $n/k$ in the sum is smaller than $n$. So $f^{-1}(n)=-\frac1{f(1)}\sum_{k\mid n,k>1}f(k)f^{-1}(n/k)$ is determined by $f^{-1}$ at smaller arguments: computing $f^{-1}(1),f^{-1}(2),f^{-1}(3),\dots$ in order defines it.

solutions.title: Uniqueness
solutions.body: Suppose $g_1$ and $g_2$ are both inverses of $f$. Using associativity, commutativity and the identity $\epsilon$: $g_1=g_1*\epsilon=g_1*(f*g_2)=(g_1*f)*g_2=\epsilon*g_2=g_2$. ∎

prompt: For real functions $f,g$ defined on the positive integers, their *Dirichlet convolution* is $(f*g)(n)=\sum_{k\mid n}f(k)\,g(n/k)$, the sum over all positive divisors $k$ of $n$. The function $\epsilon$ is $\epsilon(1)=1$ and $\epsilon(n)=0$ for $n\ne1$; $\mathbf 1(n)=1$ for all $n$; $U$ is the set of real functions $f$ with $f(1)\ne0$; and $f^{-1}$ is an inverse of $f$ if $f*f^{-1}=\epsilon$. The *Möbius function* $\mu$ is the inverse of $\mathbf 1$: $\sum_{k\mid n}\mu(k)=\epsilon(n)$ for all $n$. Find $\mu(n)$ when $n=1$, $n=p$ is prime, $n=p^2$ is the square of a prime, and $n=p_1p_2$ is a product of two distinct primes.

For real functions $f,g$ defined on the positive integers, their *Dirichlet convolution* is $(f*g)(n)=\sum_{k\mid n}f(k)\,g(n/k)$, the sum over all positive divisors $k$ of $n$. The function $\epsilon$ is $\epsilon(1)=1$ and $\epsilon(n)=0$ for $n\ne1$; $\mathbf 1(n)=1$ for all $n$; $U$ is the set of real functions $f$ with $f(1)\ne0$; and $f^{-1}$ is an inverse of $f$ if $f*f^{-1}=\epsilon$. The Möbius function $\mu$ satisfies $\sum_{k\mid n}\mu(k)=\epsilon(n)$ for all $n$. Use induction to find $\mu(p_1p_2\cdots p_\ell)$ for distinct primes $p_1,\dots,p_\ell$.

solutions.title: Induction on $\ell$
solutions.body: Claim: $\mu(p_1\cdots p_\ell)=(-1)^\ell$. For $\ell=0,1$ this is $\mu(1)=1$, $\mu(p)=-1$. Suppose it holds for fewer than $\ell$ primes and let $n=p_1\cdots p_\ell$ with $\ell\ge1$. The divisors of $n$ correspond to subsets of $\{p_1,\dots,p_\ell\}$; those with $j$ primes number $\binom\ell j$ and have $\mu=(-1)^j$ for $j<\ell$ by the induction hypothesis. Since $\sum_{k\mid n}\mu(k)=0$, $$\mu(n)=-\sum_{j=0}^{\ell-1}\binom\ell j(-1)^j=-\Big[(1-1)^\ell-(-1)^\ell\Big]=(-1)^\ell.$$ ∎

prompt: For real functions $f,g$ defined on the positive integers, their *Dirichlet convolution* is $(f*g)(n)=\sum_{k\mid n}f(k)\,g(n/k)$, the sum over all positive divisors $k$ of $n$. The function $\epsilon$ is $\epsilon(1)=1$ and $\epsilon(n)=0$ for $n\ne1$; $\mathbf 1(n)=1$ for all $n$; $U$ is the set of real functions $f$ with $f(1)\ne0$; and $f^{-1}$ is an inverse of $f$ if $f*f^{-1}=\epsilon$. The Möbius function $\mu$ satisfies $\sum_{k\mid n}\mu(k)=\epsilon(n)$ for all $n$, and $\mu(p_1\cdots p_\ell)=(-1)^\ell$ for distinct primes. Determine $\mu(n)$ when the prime factorization of $n$ contains a repeated prime, and summarize $\mu$ in a single expression with cases.
answer: $\mu(n)=0$ if some prime squared divides $n$; $\mu(n)=(-1)^\ell$ if $n$ is a product of $\ell$ distinct primes (including $\mu(1)=1$)

solutions.title: Check a candidate and use uniqueness
solutions.body:
Define $\mu'(n)=(-1)^\ell$ if $n$ is a product of $\ell\ge0$ distinct primes and $\mu'(n)=0$ if a prime square divides $n$. For $n>1$ with distinct primes $q_1,\dots,q_r$ ($r\ge1$), the divisors $k$ of $n$ with $\mu'(k)\ne0$ are the products of subsets of $\{q_i\}$, so $\sum_{k\mid n}\mu'(k)=\sum_{j=0}^r\binom rj(-1)^j=(1-1)^r=0$, and for $n=1$ the sum is $1$. Thus $\mu'*\mathbf1=\epsilon$, so $\mu'$ is an inverse of $\mathbf1$, and by uniqueness of inverses (problem 2c) $\mu=\mu'$.

So $\mu(n)=0$ when $n$ has a repeated prime factor, and $$\mu(n)=\begin{cases}(-1)^\ell&n\text{ a product of }\ell\text{ distinct primes}\\0&n\text{ has a repeated prime factor.}\end{cases}$$

**Answer: as above**

prompt: For real functions $f,g$ defined on the positive integers, their *Dirichlet convolution* is $(f*g)(n)=\sum_{k\mid n}f(k)\,g(n/k)$, the sum over all positive divisors $k$ of $n$. The function $\epsilon$ is $\epsilon(1)=1$ and $\epsilon(n)=0$ for $n\ne1$; $\mathbf 1(n)=1$ for all $n$; $U$ is the set of real functions $f$ with $f(1)\ne0$; and $f^{-1}$ is an inverse of $f$ if $f*f^{-1}=\epsilon$. Let $\mu$ be the Möbius function (the inverse of $\mathbf1$; $\mu(n)=(-1)^\ell$ for a product of $\ell$ distinct primes, $0$ if a prime square divides $n$). There exists a function $f$ such that $\sum_{k\mid n}f(k)=n^2$ for all positive integers $n$. Find $f(2^43^4)$.

solutions.title: Invert with $\mu$
solutions.body:
The condition says $\mathbf1*f=N$ where $N(n)=n^2$. Convolving with $\mu$: $f=\mu*(\mathbf1*f)=\mu*N$, so $$f(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)\left(\frac nd\right)^2.$$ For $n=2^43^4$ only $d=1,2,3,6$ have $\mu(d)\ne0$: $$f(n)=n^2-\left(\tfrac n2\right)^2-\left(\tfrac n3\right)^2+\left(\tfrac n6\right)^2=2^83^8-2^63^8-2^83^6+2^63^6=2^63^6(36-9-4+1)=2^63^6\cdot24=2^93^7=1{,}119{,}744.$$

**Answer: $2^9\cdot3^7=1{,}119{,}744$**

answer: Any function lying in two of the three sets must equal $\epsilon$.

solutions.title: Check the three pairs
solutions.body:
- $U_s\cap U_m$ and $U_s\cap U_a$: a function in $U_s$ vanishes for $n>1$, and in $U_m$ or $U_a$ it has $f(1)=1$; so it is $\epsilon$.

e0$; $U_m$ (multiplicative): $f(1)=1$ and $f(mn)=f(m)f(n)$ whenever $\gcd(m,n)=1$; $U_a$ (anti-multiplicative): $f(1)=1$ and $f(p^k)=0$ for every prime $p$ and integer $k\ge1$. Show that any $f\in U$ with $f(1)=1$ can be written as $f=g*h$ with $g\in U_m$ and $h\in U_a$. (Hint: construct a multiplicative $g$ such that $h=g^{-1}*f$ is anti-multiplicative.)
answer: Take $g$ multiplicative with $g(p^k)=f(p^k)$; then $h=g^{-1}*f$ vanishes on prime powers.

solutions.title: Build $g$ from the prime-power values of $f$
solutions.body: Define $g$ by $g(1)=1$ and $g(p_1^{k_1}\cdots p_\ell^{k_\ell})=\prod_i f(p_i^{k_i})$. Then $g(1)=1$ and $g(mn)=g(m)g(n)$ for coprime $m,n$, so $g\in U_m$, and $g(p^k)=f(p^k)$. The inverse $g^{-1}$ exists by problem 2c with $g^{-1}(1)=1$. Let $h=g^{-1}*f$. Then $h(1)=g^{-1}(1)f(1)=1$, and for a prime power, $$h(p^k)=\sum_{i=0}^kg^{-1}(p^i)f(p^{k-i})=\sum_{i=0}^kg^{-1}(p^i)g(p^{k-i})=(g^{-1}*g)(p^k)=\epsilon(p^k)=0\quad(k\ge1).$$ So $h\in U_a$, and $f=g*h$. ∎

e0$; $U_m$ (multiplicative): $f(1)=1$ and $f(mn)=f(m)f(n)$ whenever $\gcd(m,n)=1$; $U_a$ (anti-multiplicative): $f(1)=1$ and $f(p^k)=0$ for every prime $p$ and integer $k\ge1$. Suppose $n$ has prime factorization $p_1^{k_1}\cdots p_\ell^{k_\ell}$ with each $k_i\ge1$ (so $\ell$ is the number of distinct primes), and let $k$ be the exponent of $2$ in $n$ ($k=0$ if $n$ is odd). Define $$F(n)= egin{cases}\ell(\ell-1)+2&k\ge2\(\ell-1)^2+2&k=1\ rac{\ell(\ell-1)}2+1&k=0.\end{cases}$$ Determine a multiplicative function $G\in U_m$ and an anti-multiplicative function $H\in U_a$ such that $G*H=F$.
answer: $G(n)=\gcd(2,n)$ (so $G(n)=2$ for even $n$, $1$ for odd $n$) and $H(n)=1$ if $n=1$ or $n$ is a product of two distinct primes, $H(n)=0$ otherwise

solutions.title: Read off $G$ on prime powers, then guess $H$
solutions.body:
If $F=G*H$ with $H\in U_a$, then on prime powers $F(p^k)=\sum_{j}H(p^j)G(p^{k-j})=G(p^k)$ (as $H(p^j)=0$ for $j\ge1$). Now $F(2^k)=2$ for $k\ge1$ (for $\ell=1$: $0+2$ if $k\ge2$, $0+2$ if $k=1$) and $F(p^k)=1$ for odd $p$. So the multiplicative $G$ is $G(n)=2$ if $n$ is even and $1$ if $n$ is odd, i.e. $G(n)=\gcd(2,n)$.

The odd case $F(n)=\binom\ell2+1$ suggests that $H$ counts pairs of distinct prime factors, so try $H(n)=1$ for $n=1$ and for $n$ a product of two distinct primes, and $0$ otherwise (this is in $U_a$). Then $(G*H)(n)=G(n)+\sum_{\{p,q\}}G(n/pq)$, summed over pairs of distinct primes dividing $n$.
- $k=0$ ($n$ odd): $G=1$ everywhere, so $1+\binom\ell2$. ✓
- $k\ge2$: $n/pq$ is always even, so $2+2\binom\ell2=\ell(\ell-1)+2$. ✓
- $k=1$: the $\ell-1$ pairs containing $2$ give an odd $n/pq$ (value $1$) and the $\binom{\ell-1}2$ other pairs give value $2$: $2+(\ell-1)+(\ell-1)(\ell-2)=(\ell-1)^2+2$. ✓

**Answer: $G(n)=\gcd(2,n)$; $H(n)=1$ if $n=1$ or $n=pq$ with $p\ne q$ prime, else $0$**
